analysis.one_liner: Wipes out federal guidance protecting LGBTQ workers from workplace harassment and discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 6 cosponsors in March 2024, was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare two Equal Employment Opportunity Commission documents null and void: a 2023 proposed guidance on workplace harassment and a 2021 fact sheet explaining that federal law bars employment discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. It would also bar the EEOC from ever issuing similar guidance. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025. [S2][S4]
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be employers facing workplace discrimination and harassment claims, since the EEOC would lose the documents it uses to explain and enforce workers' protections based on sexual orientation, gender identity, and harassment generally, and could not issue similar ones again. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: The bill would nullify the EEOC's proposed 2023 harassment guidance and its 2021 fact sheet on sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination, giving employers a legal landscape with less agency guidance they could be held to in discrimination cases.

It would go further than a simple repeal by permanently barring the EEOC from issuing any 'identical or substantially similar' guidance or fact sheet, preventing future commissions from reissuing these protections.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear the cost, especially LGBTQ workers. The EEOC's guidance documents are how the agency tells workers what harassment and discrimination are illegal and how to bring a claim; nullifying them would leave workers with fewer clear federal standards, and the ban on similar future guidance would lock that in. [S2]

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the guidance would strip workers of the agency's plain-language explanation of what counts as illegal harassment and discrimination, making it harder for people to know and enforce their rights.
The prohibition on 'substantially similar' future guidance would prevent the EEOC from updating its interpretation as courts decide new cases, freezing enforcement standards in place.

Even supporters of the bill acknowledged in its design that it targets agency guidance documents rather than the underlying statute, so the Supreme Court's Bostock ruling and Title VII would still apply in court; the bill would mainly reduce the practical enforcement help the agency offers workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers, the benefit is reduced exposure to EEOC enforcement built on these guidance documents. For workers, the cost is the loss of clear federal standards on harassment and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, plus a permanent ban on similar guidance. The cost to workers outweighs the employer benefit, and the bill never advanced far enough for that trade to be tested in a vote. [S2][S4]

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late March 2024 and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, it sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Ogles introduced the bill on March 21, 2024, joined by six Republican cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in the House or Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who rely on the EEOC's harassment and anti-discrimination guidance are better off, because those documents remain in effect and the ban on similar guidance never became law. No employer relief was achieved.

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ogles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the EEOC harassment guidance and the sexual orientation and gender identity fact sheet.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be guessed from sponsorship: all seven supporters were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored.

industries.industry: Employers facing discrimination and harassment claims
industries.note: Nullifying the EEOC's guidance and barring similar future guidance would weaken the standards used to police workplace harassment and sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination, reducing enforcement exposure for employers. Workers would lose the corresponding protections.

industries.industry: Employment law practitioners and compliance consultants
industries.note: Removing agency guidance would leave more legal questions to be settled case by case in litigation, increasing uncertainty and legal costs for businesses and workers alike.
